articles.title: How Niger restored 5 million hectares without planting a single tree
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM In 1983, an Australian agricultural adviser named Tony Rinaudo was working in the Sahel when he noticed something that didn’t fit the picture everyone had of the region. The land looked barren. But beneath the depleted soil, root systems were still alive. When farmers eased the pressure of overgrazing, […]
The post How Niger restored 5 million hectares without planting a single tree first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

In 1983, an Australian agricultural adviser named Tony Rinaudo was working in the Sahel when he noticed something that didn’t fit the picture everyone had of the region. The land looked barren. But beneath the depleted soil, root systems were still alive. When farmers eased the pressure of overgrazing, green shoots came up.

Rinaudo had found something that would eventually restore five million hectares (about 12.4 million acres) of savanna in Niger without a single seedling being planted. The trees weren’t gone. They were waiting underground.

The technique is called Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration, or FMNR. Farmers identify which shoots are emerging from existing root systems to protect and which to prune. The process is slow, deliberate, and entirely driven by the people who own the land. Because the trees belong to the farmers, they provide direct value: shade, erosion control, firewood, fruit, animal fodder. Protection is self-interest, not a program obligation.

All about the numbers

Niger formally recognized FMNR as a national soil restoration method in 2020. By then, the World Agroforestry Centre and the NDC Partnership estimated more than 200 million trees had been restored across five million hectares, benefiting roughly 2.5 million people.

The broader context is Africa’s AFR100 initiative, in which 33 countries committed to restoring 129 million hectares (about 319 million acres) of degraded land by 2030. The Great Green Wall runs alongside it: an 8,000-kilometer (about 5,000-mile) band of vegetation from Senegal to Djibouti through 11 Sahel countries, targeting 100 million hectares restored, 250 million tons of carbon sequestered, and 10 million new jobs. Financing runs through a $33 billion framework involving the Global Environment Facility, the African Development Bank, and the World Bank.

By mid-2026, roughly 18 percent of the 100 million hectare target had been restored, four years ahead of schedule. Conflict is slowing progress in parts of the region, though. Burkina Faso, parts of Niger, and Mali lack stable governance following coups, making long-term implementation close to impossible in those areas. At current pace, the Great Green Wall will restore roughly 40 to 50 million hectares (about 99 to 124 million acres) by 2030, less than half the target.

The lesson from Ethiopia

Ethiopia is worth looking at for contrast. The Green Legacy Initiative operates on a different model: state-organized mass planting, billions of seedlings annually. In July 2019, government-organized volunteers planted 350 million trees in a single day.

These are, undoubtedly, striking numbers. However, planting and surviving are different things. Researchers at the Ethiopian Environment and Forest Research Institute found that without follow-up care, more than half of seedlings fail to establish. Niger’s FMNR approach doesn’t have this problem: trees growing from existing root systems already have what they need to survive, and farmers have direct financial reasons to protect them. Rwanda’s TREPA project operates on similar logic, integrating trees economically into farmland through fruit trees, fodder crops, and timber. What holds across all the success cases is the same: restoration lasts when communities have economic stakes in trees, not civic obligations to tend them.

Where it goes from here

FMNR is now being tested in more than 20 countries, from Ghana to Madagascar. Experts at the World Agroforestry Centre estimate the method could work across large parts of the Sahel and southern African savanna, wherever root systems have survived without being destroyed outright.

Whether the broader initiative hits its 2030 targets depends on funding and political stability in some of the hardest places on earth to run long-term programs. The method itself is no longer in question. Five million restored hectares in Niger, with no planting, is a fairly unambiguous answer.

articles.title: UK's rarest bird of prey rears new chicks in secret location
articles.summary: The Montagu Harrier successfully nested for the second year running in the same secret location.
articles.content:
The UK's rarest bird of prey has successfully nested for the second year running in the same secret location, the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) has reported.

A male Montagu's harrier, known as "AU" by conservationists, bred with two different females, rearing six chicks across two nests on English farmland.

Montagu's harriers were put on a "red list" of birds most at risk in the UK in 2021. Numbers have declined from a high of nine successful nests in 2011, to no evidence of successful breeding between 2020 and 2024.

An RSPB spokesperson said: "We are doing our absolute utmost to save this iconic species in the UK and are delighted with six flying juveniles this year."

Four chicks hatched in the same secret location last year.

The charity said careful monitoring, in partnership with the farmers on whose land the birds nested, meant the nests were protected by fences to exclude ground predators such as foxes.

The single male Montagu's harrier has also been working very hard to keep his two nests of hungry chicks fed.

The BBC was given exclusive access to the nest and was able to witness some of the spectacular feeding behaviour of the raptors: the male drops prey in mid-air and the female rolls upside down to catch it in her talons.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a meaningful conservation success with the rare Montagu Harrier breeding successfully for the second consecutive year in the UK, indicating positive progress in protecting an endangered species. The story includes specific details about conservation efforts, collaboration with farmers, and the impact on the species' population, which has broad environmental significance.

**What happened** – For the second year in a row, a male Montagu Harrier, called "AU" by conservationists, has raised six chicks with two different females. This happened on English farmland at a secret location protected by the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB). The nests were carefully guarded with fences to keep out predators like foxes. The BBC was even allowed to film the male feeding the chicks in a special way.

**Impact** – This successful breeding is important because it shows that conservation efforts can help bring back a species that was struggling. The fact that six young birds have grown strong enough to fly means there is hope for increasing the Montagu Harrier population in the UK. Protecting the nests and working closely with farmers made this success possible.

**What's next step** – The RSPB will continue monitoring the birds and protecting their nests. They plan to keep working with farmers to create safe spaces for these rare harriers to breed. This may lead to more successful nests and a stronger population in the future.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Careful protection and teamwork have helped the UK’s rarest bird of prey raise chicks successfully for two years in a row.

articles.title: Scientists discover a real-life “dragon” and name it after Syrax
articles.summary: Scientists discovered a small, yellowish mountain horned dragon in Thailand and named it Acanthosaura syrax after a dragon from House of the Dragon. Found only in a narrow band of high-elevation forest, the distinctive new species could become a flagship for protecting its rare mountain habitat.
articles.content:
Scientists have identified a new species of lizard living in the high mountain forests of western Thailand. The species, Acanthosaura syrax, takes its name from Syrax, the dragon ridden by Queen Rhaenyra Targaryen in House of the Dragon.

Acanthosaura syrax belongs to a group of agamid lizards known as mountain horned dragons, which are distinguished by the spiny crests that extend along the neck and back.

Researchers found the species in an evergreen forest within Mae Wong National Park, in Tak-Kamphaeng Phet Province, at elevations above 1,300 meters. So far, it has not been found anywhere else. Its discovery increases the number of recognized species in the genus Acanthosaura to 23.

The research was led by Poramad Trivalairat and colleagues from Chulabhorn Royal Academy and Kasetsart University. The team intentionally chose the name Syrax because several traits of the fictional dragon are reflected in the newly described lizard.

Why Scientists Chose the Name Syrax

In the fantasy series, Syrax is known for her striking yellow coloration, relatively small size compared with other dragons, and unusually high egg production.

The researchers saw similar characteristics in A. syrax. The lizard has yellowish-green coloration, ranks among the smallest species in its genus, and produces relatively large clutches of eggs for its body size. The scientists have proposed "Syrax mountain horned dragon" as its English common name, along with a Thai name that carries the same meaning.

The species is distinctive for more than its fantasy-inspired name. It has the smallest neck and back crest scales yet documented in the genus, as well as a generally small body size. Unlike several closely related species, it does not have a black patch around the eye. Instead, it has a characteristic dark collar marking.

DNA Confirms a Distinct Species

Genetic testing supported the physical differences observed by the researchers. An analysis of two genes showed that A. syrax is genetically distinct from its closest known relative, A. lepidogaster, as well as from every other recognized species in the group.

The newly identified lizard appears to occupy only a narrow zone of high-altitude forest. According to the researchers, the rugged landscape naturally separates its populations across the mountain range, which could make the species especially vulnerable if its habitat faces additional pressure.

The team is urging stronger protection for the high-elevation forests of Mae Wong. They suggest that A. syrax could become a flagship species for conservation in the region, joining other rare animals found there, including the Asian forest tortoise, Oldham's leaf turtle and the Indochinese tiger.

The study is published in the open-access journal ZooKeys.

articles.title: Living with drought has taught pastoralists lessons the world needs
articles.content:
Cattle are a central part of the identity of Andrew Msami’s Maasai community in northeast Tanzania. Herd size determines social position, and many people keep all their wealth in livestock, not banks. But in recent years, Msami and others have been forced to sell the animals and buy goats, which can handle drought better but are less financially and culturally valuable. Msami says adapting to a shifting climate has been a part of Maasai life for generations, but recent conditions represent an existential threat.

“We have to adapt because it’s like desertification is attacking our identity,” Msami told Grist. “If you lose your identity, it means you have lost everything.”

The Maasai are pastoralists, a term that describes the roughly 500 million people around the world who tend herds of livestock like cattle, goats, and sheep. They often move with the animals as they seek grass and water. Because they live and work in places with arid conditions and extreme temperatures, they are particularly vulnerable to climate change.

Around the world, drought and land degradation threaten rangelands, which make up roughly half of the planet’s landmass, and the pastoralists from Tanzania and Sudan to Nepal and Mongolia that rely on them. Desertification is occurring at 30 to 35 times the historical average, threatening even the most resilient communities. That’s on top of an influx of invasive species, extractive industries, tourists, and other threats.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

To address these overlapping crises, Msami and hundreds of other pastoralists are in Mongolia this week for the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification, or UNCCD. They are calling for stronger protections for Indigenous pastoral traditions, greater access to funding and resources to combat the crisis, and official recognition that the experience of generations living on increasingly marginal lands offers lessons for adapting to a hotter, drier world.

“We want to give the world a message that it’s not only the land that you will have to really look at,” said Msami, who is the program lead for the Pastoralists Indigenous Non-Governmental Organizations Forum, or PINGOs Forum, which is a network representing over 50 pastoralist organizations in Tanzania. “But you look at the people in that land, and maybe their lives should not be disturbed or sacrificed for the development of the world.”

That message must first overcome a global environmental movement that has not always prioritized rangelands and the peoples who steward them.

In 1992, world leaders gathered at the historic United Nations Earth Summit in Brazil, where they identified three great environmental challenges: climate change, biodiversity loss, and desertification. Global conferences were established for each, creating a forum where the world would develop plans to tackle them. In the decades since, trillions of dollars have flowed toward the first two, while desertification has largely been relegated to a problem for the developing world to address.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

“But now the history is catching them because when you look at Spain, France, even Sweden, all those countries, they have a bigger drought ever since the last two years,” said Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim, who is Mbororo from Chad and the first chair of the Indigenous peoples caucus at UNCCD. “So it is becoming a developed countries issue, and now they start paying more attention, but still it does not get the same attention on the level of political will or finance.”

Although this is the 17th meeting of the convention, Ibrahim described this year’s event as “unique, historic, and particular.” That is because it is the first with a formal caucus specifically for Indigenous peoples, something not found at the climate and biodiversity conferences. Because of that, Ibrahim and others consider this gathering a unique opportunity for Indigenous pastoralists to advocate for their rights and advance their goals on the international stage.

The gathering also comes during the United Nations’ International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists, which Ibrahim said has had a positive impact on raising awareness of the challenges communities like his face and the contributions they are making to climate resilience.

Despite those signs of progress, attendees in Mongolia said that the Indigenous caucus has faced resistance. In the first week of the conference, Ibrahim led a protest to demand full participation for the caucus and for its official functions to be established.

As the world increasingly works to address drought, Ibrahim and others are concerned that, after decades of being overlooked, a global focus could sideline them even further. About a third of Mongolia’s population practice pastoral lifestyles, for example, but often have no role in global climate discussions.

Some countries have responded to drought and land degradation by restricting pastoralist herd sizes and restricting movement. That comes despite scientific evidence that pastoralism boosts biodiversity and supports climate resilient landscapes, among other benefits.

But Ibrahim said that the rate of desertification has accelerated beyond the point where traditional knowledge alone is enough. She said that in Chad the desert is advancing 2 kilometers, or 1.2 miles, each year. “We have the land degradation very, very fast, and of course we use our knowledge to try to restore the land,” she said. “We try to fix it, but it is still there.”

That’s why a call for greater legal protections and resources for their livelihoods is central to this year’s conference. “Securing land and mobility rights is not separate from climate adaptation,” said Solange Bandiaky-Badji, who is coordinator and president of the Rights and Resources Initiative, a global coalition of over 200 organizations focused on land rights. “It is a fundamental part of building resilience.”

Bandiaky-Badji said the rest of the world should learn about climate adaptation and resilience from pastoralists. But, she said, none of their expertise and experiences matter unless countries protect rights to land and mobility. The right to free, prior, and informed consent, which requires that Indigenous peoples have a say in what occurs on their lands and in their waters, is one that Bandiaky-Badji said needs greater enforcement. Because pastoralists are mobile, their land rights are not always recognized, and pastoralist leaders often do not receive an invitation to negotiate agreements and solutions.

Both Ibrahim and Bandiaky-Badji said global climate change and biodiversity conferences should follow the UNCCD’s focus on active inclusion of Indigenous voices.

But beyond that, Bandiaky-Badji said desertification and rangelands can no longer be treated as secondary issues. “There is a link between climate resilience, protecting biodiversity, and restoring landscapes,” she said. “They’re all interrelated. And until we start seeing them as interrelated, we might have these different COPs, but it will not really solve the systemic problem that we have been dealing with. And the climate crisis is a systemic problem that we need to deal with.”

articles.personality_title: Indigenous pastoralists lead new efforts to fight desertification and climate change
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Pastoralists are people who raise animals like cattle, goats, and sheep and often move with their herds to find food and water. Many live in dry areas that are becoming hotter and drier because of climate change. This makes it harder for them to keep their animals and way of life.

**What happened** – Leaders from pastoralist communities around the world met in Mongolia for a United Nations meeting called the Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD). They shared their experiences living with drought and asked for more support, such as legal protections for their land and money to help them adapt. This year’s meeting was special because it was the first time Indigenous peoples had their own official group at the event.

**Impact** – This meeting is important because it recognizes the knowledge and struggles of pastoralists who have adapted to harsh environments for generations. It also brings attention to desertification, which has often been ignored compared to climate change and biodiversity loss. Supporting pastoralists can help protect land, improve biodiversity, and strengthen communities facing climate risks.

**What's next step** – The pastoralists and their supporters want governments to give them more rights to their land and freedom to move their herds. They also hope other global climate meetings will include Indigenous voices like the UNCCD does. This could lead to better policies that protect both people and nature in dry areas.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Indigenous pastoralists are gaining recognition for their vital role in fighting desertification and adapting to climate change through new international cooperation and legal support.

articles.personality_title_es: Los pastores indígenas lideran nuevos esfuerzos contra la desertificación y el cambio climático
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los pastores son personas que crían animales como ganado, cabras y ovejas y a menudo se mueven con sus rebaños para encontrar comida y agua. Muchos viven en zonas secas que se están volviendo más calientes y áridas debido al cambio climático. Esto dificulta mantener sus animales y su forma de vida.

**Qué pasó** – Líderes de comunidades pastorales de todo el mundo se reunieron en Mongolia para una reunión de las Naciones Unidas llamada Convención para Combatir la Desertificación (UNCCD). Compartieron sus experiencias con la sequía y pidieron más apoyo, como protecciones legales para sus tierras y fondos para ayudarles a adaptarse. Esta reunión fue especial porque fue la primera vez que los pueblos indígenas tuvieron un grupo oficial.

**Impacto** – Esta reunión es importante porque reconoce el conocimiento y las dificultades de los pastores que han vivido en ambientes difíciles durante generaciones. También pone atención en la desertificación, que a menudo ha sido ignorada en comparación con el cambio climático y la pérdida de biodiversidad. Apoyar a los pastores puede ayudar a proteger la tierra, mejorar la biodiversidad y fortalecer a las comunidades ante los riesgos climáticos.

**Próximo paso** – Los pastores y sus apoyos quieren que los gobiernos les den más derechos sobre sus tierras y la libertad de mover sus rebaños. También esperan que otras reuniones climáticas globales incluyan las voces indígenas como lo hace la UNCCD. Esto podría llevar a mejores políticas que protejan tanto a las personas como a la naturaleza en las zonas secas.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Los pastores indígenas están ganando reconocimiento por su papel vital en la lucha contra la desertificación y la adaptación al cambio climático gracias a una nueva cooperación internacional y apoyo legal.
